verdict.headline: A global bond selloff opens September, with Japan's benchmark yield at a 30-year high
verdict.label: Japan's 10Y hits 3% for the first time since 1996; US 30Y trades above 5.30%, gilts clear 5.2%, Bund at a 2011 high. Brent $91.28 after two supertankers were struck in Hormuz. Dow futures -335. ISM and JOLTS today.
verdict.rationale_short: The oil-inflation impulse from the Strait of Hormuz is being paid for at the long end of every developed bond market at once, not in equities: Japan's 10-year reached 3% for the first time since 1996, the US 30-year traded through the 5.30% level it has never closed above, and gilts cleared 5.2%. The mechanism is term premium and repatriation rather than growth — Japanese institutions hold the largest foreign Treasury position, and domestic 30-year paper near 4.18% changes what that position is worth. A US 30-year close above 5.30% marks the level crossed; a close back under 5.25% says the buyback bid is still absorbing supply.

supporting_data.label: Japan's 10-year JGB reaches 3% for the first time since 1996; 20-year at 3.885%, 30-year set for a record 4.18% close
US 30-year bond enters September on its worst stretch since 2006, with the yield above 5.30%
Global bond rout spreads: UK gilts past 5.2%, Germany's 10-year at 3.34%, the highest since 2011
Two supertankers carrying Saudi crude struck by projectiles minutes apart in the Strait of Hormuz; Brent $91.28
Dow futures shed 335 points (-0.6%), S&P 500 futures -0.6%, Nasdaq-100 futures -1.2% before the open
CME FedWatch puts September 15-16 hike odds at 66.1%, roughly double the pre-Jackson Hole level

watchlist_mentions.note: Down about 1% premarket with the semiconductor group as yields rose; no company news since Monday's reclaim of $220. The move is rate-sensitivity rather than anything Blackwell-specific, which makes a 30Y close back under 5.25% the condition that unwinds it.
Off more than 1% premarket alongside NVDA and AMD, with SMH down over 1%. Memory carries the highest duration sensitivity in the complex because the AI-capex earnings stream is furthest out.

Brent at $91.28 (+0.87%), up 8.96% over the past month, after two supertankers carrying Saudi crude were struck in the Omani corridor. The $94.00 regime trigger sits $2.72 above spot; energy was the only sector bid in premarket for a second session.

$4,456.86, near a two-week low and down a second consecutive session into an escalation. Gold falling while yields rise says the market is pricing the Hormuz strikes as an inflation event, not a risk event — the same cross-asset signature as Monday.

$78,616.87 (+0.80%), holding above the $76,661 August 24 structural support through the overnight rout. It has not reclaimed the $80,000 level lost last week; Treasury buyback operations begin September 9.
15.18 (+5.20%). Higher, but with no event premium priced into a week carrying ISM, ADP, ISM Services and Friday payrolls — the equity market has still not marked the rate move.

trade_setups.thesis: The long bond traded above 5.30% during the overnight rout but has never closed there. Bloomberg records the worst run into September since 2006, and the marginal seller is now foreign: Japanese institutions holding the largest foreign Treasury position face domestic 30-year paper near 4.18%. Whether the level is a ceiling or a floor is decided by a settlement print, not an intraday tag.
trade_setups.entry: The levels that define it: a daily close above 5.30% marks the line crossed; a close back under 5.25% says the buyback bid, with operations beginning September 9, is still absorbing supply.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close under 5.25% with Brent back below $88 on a Hormuz de-escalation.
trade_setups.horizon: Today's 4:00 PM ET settlement, then Friday's payrolls print.

trade_setups.asset: ISM Manufacturing (10:00 AM ET) against Monday's Chicago PMI
trade_setups.thesis: Consensus is 55.2 for August against 55.6 in July, which would be the eighth consecutive month of expansion. Monday's Chicago PMI printed 47.1 versus 57.9 expected, the weakest reading of 2026. The two cannot both be describing the national factory economy, and the prices-paid component is where the oil pass-through appears first. JOLTS at 9:00 AM ET is forecast at 7.330M against 7.359M prior.
trade_setups.entry: A national print near 55 makes Chicago a regional outlier and leaves the hike path intact; a sub-50 print makes Chicago the signal and adds the growth leg to a stagflation read.
trade_setups.invalidation: A soft ISM alongside a JOLTS undershoot below 7.2M, which would pull hike odds back under 50%.
trade_setups.horizon: Resolves today between 9:00 and 10:30 AM ET.

trade_setups.asset: The Japan repatriation channel — JGB 10Y at 3%, USD/JPY at 159.75
trade_setups.thesis: Japan's 10-year touched 3% for the first time since 1996 and the 30-year is set for a record close near 4.18%. Rising domestic yields reduce the incentive for Japanese institutions to hold foreign duration, and their Treasury position is the largest of any foreign holder. The yen is the variable that decides whether the incentive becomes a flow: at 159.75, unhedged foreign carry still pays.
trade_setups.entry: A weak yen alongside 3%-plus JGB yields keeps the Treasury bid in place; a yen rally through 155 with JGB yields still rising is the combination that pulls the money home.
trade_setups.invalidation: The Bank of Japan signalling a slower tightening path, which would take the 10-year back under 2.85%.

bear_case: The read treats this as a term-premium event, and the stronger case is that it is a growth event wearing a rate costume. Monday's Chicago PMI at 47.1 was the weakest print of 2026, and if ISM confirms it at 10:00 AM ET, the long end is rising into a contracting factory economy — the configuration in which equity multiples compress without any offsetting earnings growth. The offsetting argument is that a 66.1% hike probability is a market pricing tightening it can absorb, and the S&P closed August up 2.96%. If the 30-year closes back under 5.25% and the S&P holds 7,650 through Friday's payrolls, this read no longer holds.
